title: Twin Rivers Paper Company LLC v. Securities and Exchange Commission
lead: A securities rule lets investment companies move shareholder reports online while preserving requested paper delivery. Consumers and paper suppliers challenge the change, but encounter different barriers to obtaining judicial review.

actors.name: Consumer Action
actors.role: Membership organization asserting harm to its members.

actors.name: Twin Rivers Paper Company and three industry organizations

proceedings: The petitioners sought direct review of the SEC rule in the D.C. Circuit.
The unanimous panel denied the petition without deciding the rule’s substantive validity.
limits: This account transforms the canonical historical brief and makes no fresh opinion audit or current-regulation claim. Pinpoints use official slip pages. The result did not establish that every minor time expenditure fails Article III or that only intended statutory beneficiaries may sue.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The SEC changes the delivery default
sections.cue: What remained available to shareholders who wanted paper?
paragraphs: Investment companies, including mutual funds, generally mailed shareholder reports unless an investor chose electronic delivery. The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Rule 30e-3 to let companies instead post reports online and mail notices announcing their availability. Investors could still request paper reports. The agency projected about $140 million in annual savings, ordinarily benefiting investors because printing expenses came from fund assets, and found that many shareholders preferred online access.

An extended transition required continuing paper delivery until no earlier than January 1, 2021, with advance warnings. After a switch, each report required mailed notice giving a toll-free number for requesting that report or all future reports on paper. A requested copy had to be sent within three business days without charge.

sections.title: Consumers and paper suppliers petition for review
sections.cue: Why did their different interests matter?
paragraphs: Consumer Action, a nonprofit membership organization, joined Twin Rivers Paper Company and three industry organizations in a direct appellate challenge. They invoked the Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Investment Company Act of 1940, and Administrative Procedure Act. Among their objections was inadequate protection of shareholders who preferred paper. The industry petitioners anticipated reduced paper demand; Consumer Action claimed injury to members.

Judge Katsas wrote for a D.C. Circuit panel with Judges Henderson and Rogers. The court first examined whether Consumer Action had established a member with constitutional standing. Direct review required evidence in the agency record or supplemental material. Where standing was not apparent, the opening brief needed both argument and evidence so opponents could respond. That judicial-review requirement did not impose Article III standing on participants in agency rulemaking.

sections.title: Consumer Action’s opening evidence does not identify an injured member
sections.cue: Why did the reply affidavits arrive too late?
paragraphs: Consumer Action supplied no individual member affidavits with its opening brief. Its organizational affidavit referred broadly to members, followers, supporters, retirees, and community organizations, without identifying an injured member or clearly explaining membership. General preferences and burdens were insufficient; assertions in the brief were not evidence. Agency comments about readership, transparency, and access likewise did not connect those concerns to identified members.

The organization supplied member affidavits in reply. The deadline was not an inflexible jurisdictional rule: good cause could excuse delay when a litigant reasonably thought its first evidence sufficient or standing apparent. Neither explanation fit these vague initial submissions. In an earlier airport-expansion case, opening affidavits had identified nearby residents, and reply affidavits clarified foreseeable noise injury. Consumer Action had supplied no comparable foundation.

The reply also changed the theory. None of its affiants claimed the initially suggested impairment in access to or understanding of information. Some expressed ideological opposition; others complained of time spent making a free call. Ideological disagreement with administration of law was not concrete injury. Lost time posed a closer question, but the organization identified no pertinent statutory protection against making the call or traditional analogue supporting this theory. Presenting these debatable questions only in reply deprived opponents of the ordinary response. The court could not find standing on that showing.

sections.title: The suppliers’ commercial interest falls outside the securities statutes
sections.cue: When may someone other than an intended beneficiary sue?
paragraphs: The industry’s alleged economic loss raised a different issue: whether its interests fell within the statutes’ zone of interests. The Supreme Court’s Lexmark decision had recast that inquiry as identifying who may invoke a cause of action, rather than prudential standing. It applied to direct agency review too. An intended beneficiary could qualify, but so could a suitable challenger whose interests aligned systematically with beneficiaries’ interests.

The review provisions also mattered. Each securities statute allowed review of certain SEC orders, but “order” included rules under the Securities Act and Investment Company Act, not the Exchange Act. The Administrative Procedure Act neither independently supplied jurisdiction nor enlarged those particular review routes.

Investors were the protected beneficiaries. Paper sellers preferred more paper regardless of investors’ interests; investors might instead prefer online reports and lower expenses. Occasional agreement with a paper-preferring investor did not establish systematic alignment, and the potential conflict could grow with internet use.

The suppliers cited competitor cases allowing enforcement of statutory entry boundaries. Those challengers’ incentives were confined to guarding a specific congressional restriction. Broad requirements involving public interest, investor protection, efficiency, competition, and capital formation did not similarly channel paper sellers. Applying its precedents concerning waste treatment and pollution equipment, the court found this mismatch disqualifying.

sections.title: The petition ends without a ruling on electronic delivery’s merits
sections.cue: What did the judgment actually leave in place?
paragraphs: On August 16, 2019, the unanimous panel denied the petition. Consumer Action had not timely established an Article III basis through evidence of member injury; the paper-industry petitioners’ interests were outside those arguably protected or regulated by the securities laws.
The court neither vacated the rule nor remanded to the agency. It did not hold that electronic delivery met every substantive statutory requirement. No judge wrote separately.
